name: Mapped-clone genome sequencing
summary: The public Human Genome Project sequenced the genome in mapped pieces cloned in bacteria, reading each with automated fluorescent machines and assembling them by computer.
description: The public consortium sequenced mapped BAC/PAC clones with automated fluorescent reads and computational assembly.
tier_reason: A major reusable result, process or system within its field; broader multi-field or multi-generation dependence on this exact referent is not established.

impact.note: A scaled-up strategy used by genome centres, with the human draft and reference as its direct successors before being superseded; implies tier 2, below reviewed tier 1.

date.basis: Date of the cited public report or documented event.

events.statement: The international public human-genome effort moved its mapped-clone sequencing strategy into full-scale production.
events.caveats: Pilot activity occurred before this date; it is not asserted as the first use or a commercial offer.

evidence.locator: p. 863, The beginning of the Human Genome Project, production phase; pp. 864–867 workflow
evidence.supports: The consortium dates full-scale production to March 1999 and describes the hierarchical workflow.

date.basis: Dates the public consortium’s production phase and procedures used for the October 2000 draft, not invention of shotgun sequencing.

events.statement: The public consortium sequenced mapped BAC/PAC clones with automated fluorescent reads and computational assembly.
events.caveats: This node is the public consortium configuration, not Celera’s whole-genome strategy or every possible way to assemble a genome.

date.basis: Date of this published account, not the date of first invention or first use.

events.caveats: This is a dated publication, not proof of first awareness, acceptance, external deployment or sale.

links.statement: The consortium cited Prober’s dye-labelled terminators among production-enabling laboratory advances.
links.timing: The demonstration reported by October 1987 precedes the later described production workflow; the demonstration’s earliest date is unresolved.

evidence.locator: p. 864, technology paragraph and reference 67; p. 867
evidence.supports: Cited advance and actual varied dye-terminator use.

links.statement: The consortium identified four-colour fluorescence detection, citing Smith et al., among the advances supporting automated reads.
links.alternatives: Production also used dye-terminators and varied detectors.
links.caveats: No claim that every centre used the 1986 apparatus.
links.timing: The demonstrated readout predates production-scale refinements.

links.statement: Genomics has no link to computing. What computing was required for assembly? This would join the DNA thread to electronics.
links.caveats: Evidence needed: Assembly methods in the 2001 papers. Needs intermediate computing entries rather than one long link.
links.finding: The genome source identifies concrete software used in sequencing analysis and assembly, providing a potential computational intermediate. It does not identify the hardware processor used or connect the specific Intel 4004 to that work. PHRED/PHRAP production use and GigAssembler draft assembly are distinct; neither is direct evidence for a 4004-to-genome link.
